item.title: Caitlin Clark calls out media’s ‘false characterization’ of her amid weeks of controversy
item.description: Caitlin Clark pushed back against what she calls false characterizations of her character, saying media coverage of her fouls isn't based in reality.
item.content:encoded:
Caitlin Clark spoke out about the media coverage of her after weeks of national controversy, claiming that outlets have made false characterizations" of who she is.

"I think there's just like a false characterization of who I am sometimes," she said in an interview with ESPN on Friday.

Controversy hit a boiling point in recent days after USA Today published an opinion piece in which the writer invoked the murder of Emmett Till while criticizing the Indiana Fever guard for falling to the floor when hit by opposing players and arguing with referees over foul calls.

CAITLIN CLARK MAKES WNBA HISTORY WITH RECORD-BREAKING GAME AFTER WEEKS OF CONTROVERSY

"And I get it, like, as a reporter or as a blogger, like you can write an opinion piece and that's your job and whatever. But at the same time, like you don't know me. Like we've never had a conversation. I get people have a job to do. But at the same time, like don't make accusations about my character and who I am when you don't know me," Clark said.

"I understand this is your job and this is your profession, and this is what you get to do. And basketball is my profession, what I get to do. And the reason I play it is when I step in between the lines, I love it. And that's what's so fun about it for me is like, I get to compete. This was always my dream. And nobody should ever try to take that away from me."

Clark said that she believes some coverage isn't "based in reality."

"I think a lot of it is like, it's not always based in reality. I feel like media and journalism have a responsibility to tell the stories and a lot of times you guys are the ones controlling the narratives about what people read and what people talk about and a lot of that is sometimes so far out of touch with what is reality."

The maelstrom of national controversy began when Clark was punched in the throat by Phoenix Mercury star Alyssa Thomas during a game in June. Referees did not call a foul in the moment, but later issued Thomas a one-game suspension after the game was over.

The incident and imagery of it ignited weeks of emotional discourse by fans and pundits across the media landscape, and often incited racial debates.

WHO IS ALYSSA THOMAS? WNBA STAR SUSPENDED FOR PUNCHING CAITLIN CLARK IN THE THROAT

Clark reflected on the throat punch and its ugly fallout.

"It seems like there's always a moment like that in every season that I've played so far... it gets exhausting, it gets frustrating... yeah it was a hard foul, it should have been dealt with in the moment, and it should have been decided what it was then and reviewed it, great, we move on. We see it happen in the NBA all the time. It's not anything more than that, it's basketball," Clark said.

"It's emotionally exhausting, it's draining, it makes your shoulders tense, because you know, people don't want to talk about the basketball, they want to stir it up and make it something else."

Clark expressed reminders to media and fans to look out for her feelings and emotional well-being on the first day of All-Star weekend on Friday.

"People forget like I have feelings... I feel things, I have emotions, I get emotional, I get frustrated, I get sad and I get upset," Clark said in an interview with Sirius XM on Friday. "Social media is not always reality and that is really lost on people... you read all these things and you're like 'oh that has to be true, that has to be what people really think of me.'

"There's going to always be people who don't always agree with your playing style and how you carry yourself, and that's okay. That might mean you're doing something right too... there's certainly days that are hard."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Clark also brought up the toll to her emotional health while addressing her interaction with former President Barack Obama on the opening day of the weekend.

"He just complimented me for the way I handle everything. Obviously with everything going on, and he's certainly someone who's been in front of the media quite a bit. And he reminded me, he's like 'I got famous in my 40s, I didn't have to do it in my 20s,'" Clark said.

"And you know, sometimes, I think people don't always realize I'm 23 or 24 years old and trying to navigate a lot of different things, while trying to play basketball at the same time. So it was cool to hear that from him. And I think honestly it's probably a good reminder to all of us to treat people with respect and treat people with grace."

item.title: WILLIAM BENNETT, JON HAGE: AI can mimic a teacher, but it cannot shepherd a soul
item.description: AI in classrooms demands ethical guardrails and character education, argue two education leaders who warn the technology cannot shepherd a student's soul.
item.content:encoded:
This summer, at the Sun Valley conference, media, tech, business, and cultural leaders gathered to discuss what is on all our minds: artificial intelligence and where it is taking us. We cannot hide from it any longer. AI will play a fundamental role in nearly everything we do, including how our children learn.

It is hard to deny the benefits. AI can tutor a struggling student at midnight, translate a lesson into a dozen languages, and free teachers from paperwork so they can spend more time with the kids in front of them. But that promise must come with caution, especially in education. New tools are never neutral. They amplify whatever values, or lack of them thereof, are already in the classroom.

That caution was underscored twice in recent weeks. The so-called Godfather of AI warned that to protect humanity from the risks it poses, AI must be infused with compassion and virtue. Around the same time, a landmark report found that top AI models will lie, cheat, and steal to reach their goals. Not by accident, but by design.

AI CHATBOTS TAKE HEAT OVER LEFT-WING BIAS: ‘NO LONGER BE CONSIDERED NEUTRAL’

Put those findings together and the lesson for education is unmistakable. A technology that can reason without a conscience is not one we should hand to children unsupervised. AI is inherently amoral. It cannot love a student, recognize the moment a child needs encouragement rather than information, or model integrity by doing right when no one is watching. It can simulate a teacher. It cannot shepherd a soul.

The danger is not simply that AI will occasionally give a wrong answer. That danger is that students raised in an AI-powered world, without a firm grounding in judgment and character, will have no framework for deciding whether the answers they receive are honest, sound, or right. A student who cannot make that judgment is not truly educated. He or she is simply dependent.

We do not raise this as outside observers. Between us two, we have spent decades in American education, one as U.S. Secretary of Education and a longtime advocate for character-based schooling, the other running one of the nation's largest networks of charter schools. We have watched technology enter the classroom before and seen school systems get its adoption right and wrong. That experience convinces us this moment demands the same discipline educators have always brought to any new influence on a child.

This is not an argument against artificial intelligence.

The right response to transformative technology is responsible integration, not exclusion. We did not ban word processors or turn students away from the internet. The challenge was never the tool itself but the absence of guardrails around its use. AI presents that same challenge today, at a far greater scale and with far higher stakes.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Recognizing that reality, we have spent recent years working with educators and technologists on part of the answer: an approach to classroom AI built on a simple premise, that any model placed in front of a child should be filtered through age-appropriate safeguards and aligned with the values of the families it serves. That is one piece of a larger project this country needs: a genuine safety layer between powerful AI systems and the students who will use them, paired with real instruction in the judgment and character required to use those systems well.

As America celebrates its 250th anniversary, embracing new technology rather than fearing it is part of the answer. But embracing it responsibly means resisting the temptation to believe the technology itself can be made virtuous enough to solve the problem for us.

It cannot, and the answer is not to make the machines more virtuous. The answer is to make the human beings operating them more virtuous. That has always been the purpose of education. The AI revolution has simply made it more urgent.

It is incumbent on all of us, students, teachers, parents, school leaders, and lawmakers alike, to demand ethical guardrails around the AI entering our classrooms: hard questions for the companies building these systems, transparency about how they are trained, and a refusal to treat safety as an afterthought. Do that work now, and ethical AI can become the gold standard in American classrooms rather than a cautionary tale we tell too late, not because the technology demands it, but because our children do.

Jon Hage is CEO of Charter Schools USA.

item.title: Slain dad's daughter knew ‘Black Swan’ ex-ballerina shot him after one call: 'She killed him, didn't she?'
item.description: Eva Benefield suspected Ashley Benefield immediately after learning her father was shot, recalling years of allegations in the custody dispute.
item.content:encoded:
When Eva Benefield's uncle Dave called with "some really bad news," she thought of one person.

"She killed him, didn’t she?" Benefield recalled asking before her uncle confirmed that her father, Doug Benefield, had been fatally shot.

Benefield said she instantly suspected her stepmother, former ballerina Ashley Benefield.

'BLACK SWAN' MURDER: SLAIN DAD'S DAUGHTER RIPS KILLER BALLERINA STEPMOM AT SENTENCING

"At that point, I knew about the countless allegations she had made against my dad," Benefield, who has documented her father's case on TikTok, told Fox News Digital.

"There was something about her that made her obsessed with the idea that my dad was not a good person," she said. "She had called the cops multiple times on my dad. She had called CPS on my dad. I knew there was no boundary and no limit — she was going to do anything she could to frame my dad in a negative light. When my uncle said, 'Your dad's been shot,' who else was he spending time with in Florida? I just knew."

In 2024, Ashley was sentenced to 20 years in prison after being convicted of manslaughter in the 2020 shooting death of her estranged husband. Now, in her memoir, "Ghost Girl: Surviving the Black Swan Murder," Benefield is reflecting on her father's death, their relationship and the years leading up to the fatal shooting.

Benefield was still in high school when her mother, Renee Benefield, died from a heart condition. As the family reeled from the loss, Doug made his daughter his top priority.

Benefield described her father as gentle, patient and endlessly curious — an artist who was always learning something new.

"Those nine months between my mom passing away and my dad marrying Ashley were probably some of the best memories I have with my dad," she said.

"We were close. I was always following his lead. He would have all of these projects in the garage, and I would just sit with him, watch him. Those nine months when it was just the two of us, we were really leaning on each other. Anything I needed, he was there for me."

More than a year before he was killed, Doug nearly walked away from his second marriage, which was plagued with problems.

"'That's it. I'm done. I've tried everything to show her that I'm a good guy, that I love her, and she just won't believe me. She keeps making these allegations against me,'" Benefield recalled him saying.

"He was going to pack up and leave," she said. "He was going to come back to Charleston."

Instead, Benefield urged her father to stay one more day so her younger sister, Emerson, could celebrate Easter with him.

"I told him, 'She's at the age where she's going to remember that,'" Benefield said. "You need to stay and be with her, and then you can come to Charleston tomorrow. He was like, ‘You’re right. We’ll open Easter baskets. I’ll be back in Charleston tomorrow.’"

"And that was it," she continued. "I think that was the one time I saw him think about leaving and say he was going to do it, and then he didn’t."

Looking back, Benefield can't help but wonder if that decision changed everything.

"I think he stayed in Florida for one too many days after that," she said.

Within a year after losing his first wife, Doug, 54, married Ashley Byers — later Ashley Benefield — a 24-year-old former swimsuit model, just 13 days after they met.

"I had just an off-putting feeling," Benefield said. "Within three days, my dad went from having no love life since my late mother died to being married to a 24-year-old. I thought they were dating casually, not married. It was the day after meeting her that I learned they were married."

Benefield said she quickly realized Ashley was "not the sweet girl she marketed herself to be." In "Ghost Girl," she described how her home became increasingly hostile after Ashley moved in.

Benefield alleged her stepmother began isolating her from her father, blaming her for household conflicts, reading her private journal, publicly embarrassing her and seeking to push her out of the family dynamic.

"I really wanted her to like me," Benefield wrote. "But I could tell she did not like me at all, and it wasn't even personal. I was just in the way."

"There were moments where I felt it was inappropriate," Benefield told Fox News Digital. "I'd come home from school, and she would be sitting in a bra and underwear on the kitchen counter, waiting for my dad to get home. She took me to the grocery store one time and showed me she had a gun in her bra. She started a screaming match between us. My dad wasn't yelling back, but she was yelling at my dad over little things I did that upset her."

Benefield said Ashley also attempted to erase her late mother.

"She came in and got rid of everything that reminded me of my mom in my room," Benefield said. "There were pictures on the walls of my mom and me. There was a letter from my mom. She took down everything. It was all gone.

"She was asking my dad to say that my mom meant nothing to him. That stung because I knew that wasn't true, but she needed to hear that. She needed to see that the house was rid of everything that reminded him of my mom. She caused a lot of arguments, and they were over little things. She was driving a wedge between my dad and me."

In 2017, Ashley launched the American National Ballet, a Charleston-based dance company. Doug threw himself into the venture. When the company collapsed later that year, Ashley returned to Florida while pregnant with Emerson.

Doug increasingly spent his time in Florida trying to repair his relationship with Ashley and be part of Emerson's life. Benefield stayed behind in Charleston to finish high school, later writing that she wanted to distance herself from the turmoil surrounding her father.

"At a certain point, I asked my dad to leave me out of their relationship," Benefield said. "I knew it wasn't going to get better. I just felt, 'I'll turn 18, and I can move out if she's still around.' That was my plan. But my dad thought things would get better. She would try to convince him that things were getting better, and he felt, 'We're finally figuring our issues out.' Then she would accuse him of all these false allegations. But I do think he felt things would turn around."

"It never got better," Benefield said.

In September 2020, Doug was killed at the Lakewood Ranch, Florida, home where Ashley was staying with her mother. The shooting came as the estranged couple was embroiled in a contentious custody dispute over their daughter. Ashley was arrested in November of that year.

Ashley claimed she shot and killed her estranged husband, 58, in self-defense, arguing she opened fire on the Navy veteran after ordering him out of her house and alleging he refused to comply and hit her in the face.

EX-BALLERINA CONVICTED OF MANSLAUGHTER IN HIGH-PROFILE 'BLACK SWAN MURDER' CASE

"I thought he was going to kill me," Ashley testified during the trial. Investigators said she showed no visible signs of physical abuse after the shooting.

Ashley accused Doug of psychologically abusing her, but prosecutors argued the allegations were unsupported by the evidence. They noted she made the allegations in an effort to gain sole custody of their daughter.

Benefield would later come face-to-face with Ashley in court.

"It was a weird feeling, knowing this was my dad's killer," Benefield said. "When I saw her, I felt, 'My dad is really dead. This is the girl who killed him.' I got angry. But I was there to get justice. I needed to show her that I'm strong and she's not going to get away with this."

During her victim impact statement, Benefield said, "What hurts me the most is not the thought of not having my dad anymore because I will always have him around in spirit. ... What breaks my heart the most is thinking about how he found you at such a vulnerable part of his life."

Ashley was charged with second-degree murder but was convicted of the lesser charge of manslaughter after nearly seven hours of deliberations. She was sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Today, Benefield said she's focused on moving forward while carrying the lessons her father left behind.

"I wish he could have gotten out of that situation," she said. "But I would want him to know that his daughter turned out OK."

item.title: Obama Presidential Center subcontractors file fresh payment claims totaling nearly $900K
item.description: Three subcontractors claim nearly $900,000 in unpaid work on Home Court, the Obama Presidential Center's basketball facility hosting WNBA All-Star events.
item.content:encoded:
Three more subcontractors that worked on the Obama Presidential Center have filed legal claims saying they are owed nearly $900,000, adding to a growing list of payment disputes surrounding the project.

The companies each filed mechanics liens against the Obama Presidential Center property, a routine legal tool used on construction projects to recover unpaid construction costs. The subcontractors claim they are owed money for structural steel, excavation and concrete, and gymnasium flooring work performed on Home Court, the Center's 60,000-square-foot basketball and events facility.

Structural steel subcontractor Area Erectors is seeking nearly $620,000, excavation and concrete subcontractor CSI 3000 — the only Minority Business Enterprise (MBE) of the three — claims it is owed about $236,000, and gymnasium flooring specialist Floors Incorporated says it is owed nearly $25,000.

Unlike previous payment disputes reported by Fox News Digital, which largely involved work across the main campus, these claims relate specifically to Home Court, which was built under a separate construction contract. It comes as Home Court is hosting several high-profile WNBA All-Star Weekend events this week which the former president attended.

The Home Court claims are the latest in a series of subcontractor payment disputes previously reported by Fox News Digital involving the broader Obama Presidential Center project, located in Chicago's historic Jackson Park. The disputes add to a growing list of challenges during construction, including the project's ballooning cost — from an initial estimate of about $350 million to more than $1 billion — and legal challenges over contracting practices and diversity requirements.

OBAMA CENTER SUBCONTRACTOR SHUTS DOWN AMID $4M FIGHT, LAYS OFF 25

The Home Court is located at the southern end of the campus and features a regulation-size NBA basketball court, training space and multipurpose meeting and event rooms. The basketball court is decorated with phrases associated with former President Barack Obama, including "Yes we can" and "No one does big things alone."

The Obama Foundation, Obama's private nonprofit organization, oversees construction of the Obama Presidential Center. It hired Lakeside Alliance as the primary construction manager for most of the campus.

Home Court, however, was built under a separate contract by Elevate Design Builders, a joint venture led by minority-owned BOWA Construction that served as construction manager for the facility.

Although the mechanics liens are filed against the Obama Presidential Center property, they do not determine which entity is legally responsible for the disputed payments.

The newly identified liens were recorded around the time of the Obama Presidential Center's June 19 opening. The Cook County Clerk's Office told Fox News Digital there is typically a four-to-six-week delay before recorded documents appear in its online property records database, meaning they only recently became searchable online.

Elevate and the Obama Foundation did not respond to a request for comment, nor did the three subcontractors.

SUBCONTRACTORS SAY THEY’RE OWED MILLIONS, FACE FINANCIAL RUIN, AFTER HELPING BUILD OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER

Fox News Digital also identified three previously unreported mechanics liens totaling about $557,000 involving other portions of the Obama Presidential Center project.

Unlike the Home Court claims, which arise from work performed under contracts connected to Elevate Design Builders, the additional liens involve subcontractors and suppliers seeking payment further down the project's contracting chain.

For instance, O'Leary's Contractors Equipment & Supply is seeking about $184,000 in allegedly unpaid equipment rental invoices. The Cement Masons' Union Trust Funds alleges more than $326,000 in unpaid fringe benefit contributions, while Intek Construction Products is seeking about $47,000 for labor and materials it says it supplied to the project.

Jeffrey Molchan, whose company Intek Construction Products filed one of the liens, told Fox News Digital the company was seeking payment on its final invoice from another contractor and that "the project did not go as well as we anticipated in terms of the timeliness of the payment."

The additional liens involve portions of the project managed by Lakeside Alliance. In a statement, Lakeside said the Obama Presidential Center involved multiple structures, hundreds of trade partners and community businesses, and that contractual closeout continues after the center's opening. The joint venture said it remains committed to working through outstanding matters.

Fox News Digital previously reported that Black subcontractors alleged they were owed millions of dollars for work on the project, while Concrete Collective filed a mechanics lien seeking more than $40 million. The lien was later replaced by a court-approved surety bond while the underlying dispute continues in court. Adamson Plumbing also said it suspended operations and laid off workers after claiming it was left nearly $4 million in the red.

Fox News Digital also previously reported that at least four other companies filed mechanics liens during construction, while two subcontractors — Glass Management Services and Vision Painting & Decorating Services — later sought Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. Court records do not establish that the Obama Presidential Center caused those bankruptcies.

Since that reporting, two of the previously identified mechanics lien claims have been withdrawn, including one after the claimant said it recovered the amount sought through the lien, though the owner told Fox News Digital the company still lost about $200,000 on the project overall. One previously reported lien remains unresolved.

item.title: Michigan father alleges bomb threat to home after daughter spoke up about facing trans athlete without knowing
item.description: Sean Lechner says his family received an alleged bomb threat to their home after his daughter Briley spoke out about competing against a transgender athlete.
item.content:encoded:
A Michigan father says his family received alleged death threats, racist insults and threats that someone would blow up their home after he and his teenage daughter spoke publicly about her unknowingly competing against a transgender athlete in girls' volleyball.

"We've been threatened with violence, called Nazis, subjected to racist insults, and even received threats to blow up our home," Sean Lechner told Fox News Digital. "The situation became so serious that the FBI contacted us."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the FBI for comment.

VOLLEYBALL STAR SKEWERS DEMOCRAT STATE LAWMAKER FROM VIRAL SPAT AFTER 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' BILL PASSES

Lechner said his family received an "overwhelming amount of support" but also the hostile responses after he and his 16-year-old daughter, Briley, spoke out in support of protecting girls' sports. They originally spoke out last fall before resuming interviews about the situation this past week on "Fox & Friends" and with Moms for Liberty.

"All of this because I'm a father standing beside my daughter, her teammates, and every female athlete who deserves safety, privacy, fairness, and equal opportunity," the father said.

Briley, a student-athlete at Monroe High School in Michigan, said her father absorbed most of the abuse after the family went public. She has also received alleged messages accusing her of attacking transgender people and spreading hate.

"We've received death threats and threats of people coming to our house or going to my father's work," she told Fox News Digital.

"Of course, I never want to spread negativity. I don't want to spread hate or anything, and it does hurt to see that that's how people are viewing me. But I also stick to my ground, and I know what I'm standing up for, and I know what I'm battling for."

The backlash left Briley feeling as if she and her family had been abandoned by some of the adults in positions of political and educational power in her state.

"It makes me feel like I'm almost on my own, in a way," she said. "Those are the people that we expect to protect us and give us female athletes a fair game, and that's the last thing that it seems like they're prioritizing.

"For me, a 16-year-old girl, to have to be the one that speaks out about it and fights for the change, it’s just not right, in my opinion."

CALIFORNIA GIRLS' TRACK AND FIELD STARS SPEAK OUT AS GAVIN NEWSOM'S TITLE IX CRISIS GROWS

The controversy began when Briley competed against a biological male trans athlete from another school. She competed against the athlete in Fall 2024 as a freshman, and early in the 2025 season before finding out later in 2025. Fox News Digital is not disclosing any identifying information about the athlete.

Sean Lechner filed a Title IX complaint last December claiming that his daughter and her teammates had to share a locker room with the trans athlete ahead of that early-season matchup. 

"I wasn't aware that it was a male," she said.

"It was about a day or two where rumors were spread around afterwards, and my dad and I were talking about it and he said that a fellow parent and friend talked to him about it, and then my teammate started saying things."

After she found out, she said she was "devastated."

"I was devastated and, of course, concerned," Briley said. "I was very much caught off guard."

"We were asking why we weren't informed ahead of time," Briley said. "We were told that there was nothing they could do about it and that they had to protect this trans athlete."

She said she received no apology or acknowledgment from school officials.

The discovery also forced her to reflect on what she had seen across the net.

"They could jump much higher. They could swing much harder, get the ball down a lot harder, move quicker. It just seemed like they were stronger all the way around."

When Monroe played the trans athlete's team in a rematch, Briley and her teammates went into it knowing that they were facing a biological male.

"It was very weird," she said. "It was something that I knew shouldn't have been happening, and it kind of made me put my focus on that rather than just thinking about playing a regular game."

"I 100% think that knowing that there was a male on the other side mentally got in my teammates’ and my head."

Monroe lost the second matchup as well.

Briley first spoke publicly about the controversy after the season ended on Dec. 8, standing before a bank of cameras outside the Monroe County Courthouse as her father announced his Title IX complaint, with a swarm of local media in attendance to cover the controversy as it had garnered national attention throughout the season. 

"I knew that it was for the best," she said, "and I knew that fighting for female athletes is definitely what I want to continue to do."

She says the harassment began shortly after that first speaking appearance at the courthouse. 

The U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights opened investigations into Monroe and Ann Arbor Public Schools in June. The department said it would examine allegations that Monroe required female athletes to compete and share facilities with a biological male and then failed to respond appropriately to parents’ concerns.

The Michigan High School Athletic Association's policy allows the association’s executive director to determine a transgender girl’s eligibility for postseason competition on a case-by-case basis. Schools make their own regular-season participation decisions.

The national legal landscape shifted on June 30, when the Supreme Court ruled that Title IX allows schools to maintain separate boys’ and girls’ teams based on biological sex. All nine justices agreed on the Title IX question, while the court divided 6-3 on the athletes’ constitutional claims.

The decision allows states to protect sex-separated teams but does not require every state to do so. The MHSAA has said Michigan’s Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act still requires its current transgender participation policy unless state lawmakers change the law.

Briley said she recognizes that the opposing athlete may also feel targeted.

"I do feel that they might feel like we're attacking them, and it does suck that they have to be the one person that this is blowing up on," she said. "But it only takes one person."

But she also said the experience has made her more hesitant to attend college in Michigan. She hopes to play soccer at the collegiate level and now plans to examine schools’ policies before deciding where she would feel comfortable.

Sean said the threats have only strengthened the family’s resolve.

"I never imagined that simply trying to be a good father and protect my daughter would result in this level of hatred," he said. "But instead of letting that hate and anger consume us, we turned it into purpose. We leaned on our faith, stood together as a family, and dedicated ourselves to advocating for what we believe is right."

"We won't be intimidated, and we won't be silenced," he added. "We will continue to fight until my daughter—and every female athlete—has the safety, privacy, fairness, and opportunities they deserve."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Monroe Public Schools, the Michigan High School Athletic Association and Ann Arbor Public Schools for comment.

item.title: MIKE DAVIS: Why criminal referral of Jack Smith was 100% justified
item.description: Jim Jordan referred Jack Smith to the Department of Justice after his deposition allegedly omitted how he obtained congressional text messages.
item.content:encoded:
Former Biden administration special counsel Jack Smith is finally facing legal accountability for his abuse of power in his failed effort to defeat President Donald Trump's candidacy through two sham federal indictments. As part of that process, Smith provided testimony to Congress via deposition, and omitted crucial information necessary for the proper exercise of congressional oversight. House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan referred Smith to the Department of Justice for potential prosecution, and Smith should be gravely concerned.

18 U.S.C. § 1001 prohibits making knowingly and willfully false statements during government proceedings. Telling a half-truth is equivalent to making a false statement—a witness cannot omit material information and then claim his testimony was technically accurate. The congressional investigators who deposed Smith warned him of his obligation, consistent with the standard oath all witnesses take: to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, so help me God.

After President Trump left office, the Biden Justice Department obtained the contents of text messages of 44 Members of Congress, including 20 senators and 24 representatives. Those members included then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, the most powerful Republican in government. The government seized those contents while scouring phone records between President Trump, his associates, and members of Congress concerning the profoundly troubling 2020 election.

BIDEN SPECIAL COUNSEL’S 'RUNAWAY TRAIN’ SCOOPED UP SENSITIVE LAWMAKER INFO: 'ABUSE OF POWER'

During his deposition, Smith asserted that he had sought toll records through search warrants. But toll records only reveal who called whom and when. They do not reveal the contents of conversations. When asked whether he had obtained the contents of communications through a search warrant, Smith explicitly denied that he had done it. What he conveniently neglected to mention was that he had obtained the contents of those texts through the National Archives. One of Smith’s henchmen, Thomas Windom, obtained the contents of the communications without properly subjecting them to review by a "taint team" to ensure that Smith did not receive communications privileged under the Speech and Debate Clause of the Constitution.

Smith and his defenders audaciously argue that he should not be expected to read the minds of his questioners. He answered that he did not receive the texts through a search warrant, and that is all he was required to say, the Smith sycophants claim. This argument makes a mockery of the "whole truth" portion of the oath. Smith obtained the texts through a separate improper channel that Congress–through the dedicated work of Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley–uncovered just last month. That information incontrovertibly would have been essential to congressional oversight. Congress must know that the National Archives provided Smith with the contents of congressional texts, and that Smith improperly reviewed them.

Smith and his supporters also claim this referral is part of a retaliatory prosecution scheme against him, citing President Trump’s repeated calls for Smith to be held accountable. Those calls are eminently reasonable, as Smith tried to put Trump in prison for the rest of his life for exercising his First Amendment right to dispute a dubious election. Smith sought to cannibalize the Executive Branch by running roughshod over presidential immunity, a principle the Supreme Court thankfully affirmed in 2024. Requesting that the Justice Department investigate a purported crime is not retaliatory; it is consistent with the rule of law.

JACK SMITH HIT WITH CRIMINAL REFERRAL AS GOP MOVES TESTIMONY FIGHT TOWARD PROSECUTION

Some also argue that prosecuting Smith would threaten the institutional independence of the Justice Department. But the Justice Department is not independent; it is part of the Executive Branch and therefore under the control of the president. Second, Smith, while a private citizen, allegedly committed a crime. It is inconceivable how holding him legally accountable for that conduct would threaten the Justice Department. Third, with respect to alleged crimes that Smith allegedly committed while serving as a special counsel, such as conspiracy against constitutional rights under 18 U.S.C. § 241, it is proper to hold prosecutors criminally liable for unlawful conduct in the same way it is proper to hold law enforcement officers accountable. If a police officer unlawfully beats a suspect without cause and violates his civil rights, that officer should face legal accountability. Holding him accountable is not a threat to law enforcement; it is consistent with the rule of law. The same applies to rogue prosecutors like Smith.

Jack Smith is an affront to the federal government and the legal profession. He tried and failed to alter the outcome of the 2024 presidential election by prosecuting President Trump across two jurisdictions on two absurd indictments. He then withheld material information—meaning, he lied—during a congressional deposition. This information came to light only thanks to Chairman Chuck Grassley. Smith’s best hope now is to try a Clintonian "depends on the meaning of ‘is’" defense, and let a dozen jurors decide whether they will swallow it.
