item.title: Perception is reality, and the SEC needs to start winning again before it continues to puff out its chest
item.description: Nick Saban made bold claims about SEC depth at SEC Media Days, but the conference hasn't won a national championship in three straight years.
item.content:encoded:
With SEC Media Days now squarely in the rearview, each of the 16 teams from the Southeastern Conference will prepare for a pivotal year for the league.

It might sound crazy to most fans who don't have a team in the SEC, but it's been three years since the conference has won a national championship, and the natives are getting restless.

So restless, in fact, that they've resorted to all sorts of mental gymnastics about why the SEC is still the dominant conference in college football.

MISSOURI'S ELI DRINKWITZ BECOMES LATEST SEC COACH TO MAKE RIDICULOUS COMPLAINTS ABOUT BIG TEN SCHEDULES

Before I go any further, I have to point out that I am biased towards the SEC as a Florida Gator fan and I have defended the conference on numerous occasions.

But hearing some of the things being said as to why the league is still on top despite the Big Ten winning three straight natties is a bit hard to swallow, and it all culminated in the former Don of the SEC, Nick Saban, dropping this gem at Media Days on Thursday.

I want to make one thing perfectly clear: Saban is right, in a sense.

Top to bottom, the SEC is deeper than the Big Ten.

The SEC also has more talent than the Big Ten, based on both recruiting rankings and NFL Draft numbers.

The gap has closed, especially at the top, but the numbers still favor the SEC as a whole.

LANE KIFFIN MAKES RIDICULOUS EXCUSES FOR SEC'S POOR RECENT PERFORMANCE IN COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF

All of that may be true, but in college football, perception is reality, and the SEC is doing itself no favors by doing all of this talking without backing it up in the College Football Playoff.

I mentioned an SEC team hasn't won a national championship in three years, but it's even worse than that.

Last year, no team from the SEC had a win over another Power 4 program from outside of the conference in the CFP.

Alabama and Ole Miss beat Oklahoma and Georgia, respectively, but those were obviously intraconference matchups.

Sure, the SEC may still have the deepest conference top to bottom, but all the blustering from within the league just sounds like coping to any of the outsiders.

No one will take these claims seriously until the SEC gets back to the mountain top.

I reject theories like "the SEC is dead" or "The SEC and Big Ten aren't even close anymore," but fans need to acknowledge the fact that the league has some work to do to get back to its pre-2023 run of dominance.

That may never happen again, especially given the proliferation of talent in the NIL and transfer portal era, but in the meantime, the league needs to stop burying its head in the sand.

Talk is cheap. Go out there and start winning Playoff games and knocking the Big Ten from its perch.

item.title: From locker rooms to Congress: Jay Feely latest athlete seeking to take lessons in leadership to Capitol Hill
item.description: Jay Feely explains how NFL pressure prepared him for Congress as he joins a long history of athletes like Scott Turner and Tommy Tuberville in politics.
item.content:encoded:
Former NFL placekicker Jay Feely is the latest professional athlete poised to transition to a congressional career, where leadership, performing under pressure and handling public scrutiny are essential in both arenas.

Fox News Digital reached out to Feely, who spent time with the New York Giants and Arizona Cardinals before becoming an "NFL on CBS" commentator, for his take on why professional sports prepared him for public life as he seeks the seat of retiring Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz.

"Especially as a kicker — to be a successful kicker in the NFL, you have to be able to handle pressure, and you have be able handle failure. And I think those two attributes are very tangible attributes that will help you as you try to navigate the political field and try to be effective," Feely said Friday in an interview with Fox News Digital.

He said the NFL also exposed him to teammates from different backgrounds and viewpoints, helping prepare him to represent a diverse constituency.

STATE OF PLAY: DEMS BATTLE FOR SHOT AT CRUCIAL ARIZONA HOUSE SEAT AMID GOP'S RAZOR-THIN MAJORITY

"[T]he greatest advantage of being an NFL player was to be in those locker rooms where racial walls were broken down and conversations happened and you got to know people which otherwise you might not ever get to know."

He recalled rooming with LeVar Arrington and Brandon Short while with the Giants in East Rutherford, sharing stories about their different life experiences and personal views as they played chess and other games.

NFL GREAT PATRICK PETERSON SAYS LOCKER ROOM POLITICAL DISCOURSE WAS 'UNNECESSARY,' MOST PLAYERS ARE UNINFORMED

"Your job is to represent everybody and i think those experiences certainly are an asset," Feely said.

He also mentioned a trip to the infamously unfriendly confines of Lincoln Financial Field to play the Philadelphia Eagles right after the "worst game of [his] career" against the Seahawks.

The prior night he had been "spoofed" on "Saturday Night Live," and while preparing for what was a game-winning kick after an apparent icing timeout, Philadelphia played a montage of his Seattle misses on the Jumbotron to mock him.

HALL OF FAMER TONY DUNGY ENDORSES MICHELE TAFOYA IN CROWDED MINNESOTA REPUBLICAN PRIMARY FOR U.S. SENATE

"They tried to deter me, but I made the kick and my career goes on for another nine years – you learn a lot through those processes," Feely said.

Feely added that he got to know another athlete-turned-public official through their time with the NFL Players Association (NFLPA).

"There's so many different correlations with the people in sports, and a lot of the best people I know that I met in sports have thought about getting into politics," he said, reflecting on his time working with HUD Secretary Scott Turner, a former Washington Redskin.

He said he also hopes to see other athletes regardless of viewpoint who have acted on issues close to them, like former New Orleans Saints Drew Brees and Benjamin Watson.

Feely will face former state Rep. Amish Shah, D-Phoenix, who also worked for about two years as the New York Jets' team doctor.

Just over two decades ago, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner was on the NFL gridiron, playing cornerback for the Washington Redskins and then-San Diego Chargers.

The skills and lessons learned on the field helped Turner grow into his new role at HUD, which was also preceded by a stint in the Texas House of Representatives.

"The Lord used football to change the course of my life, and through the game," Turner told Fox News Digital.

"He taught me lessons that continue to guide me every day in public service: discipline, teamwork, perseverance, humility, and working toward a mission bigger than yourself."

"Those values inform how I served in the Texas state legislature and how I lead HUD today. My experience on football teams shaped how I lead, how I serve, and the example I hope to set for the next generation."

Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., had a successful mixed martial arts career before shifting from dodging fists to political blows on Capitol Hill.

Davids, who tried out for "The Ultimate Fighter," compiled a 5-1 amateur record before a brief professional MMA career in 2013, when she went 1-1.

"Turns out getting punched in the face is pretty good preparation for Congress," Davids told Fox News Digital on Friday.

She first left the octagon to support Native American communities, focusing on community development and expanding economic opportunities for Native people.

Davids later won her 2018 congressional bid in an upset against Rep. Kevin Yoder, R-Kan., in the largely red state.

"But really, fighting professionally taught me that you don't solve every challenge by throwing punches. You have to stay disciplined, work hard, respect your opponent, and keep moving forward — and that's how I approach this job, too," she told Fox News Digital.

Former Auburn Tigers Coach Tommy Tuberville transitioned to the U.S. Senate in 2021 after compiling a slew of outstanding stats as a head coach.

The Republican — now running for governor of Alabama — declined comment for this story but spoke in 2020 about the parallels between success in athletics and government.

Asked about his then-11-month campaign against incumbent Democrat Sen. Doug Jones, Tuberville told the Alabama Daily News he had to approach it at "full speed" just like a football coach.

"We put together a good, good team. And a lot of people told me when I first got started they said, coach, this is just like being a head coach. You’re only as good as the team around you," he said.

One of the most recognizable Republican figures of the last century was former HUD Secretary and former Congressman Jack Kemp.

Kemp’s political peak came in 1996 when he was the vice presidential running mate of Sen. Bob Dole, R-Kan., against President Bill Clinton.

Prior to that, Kemp led the same agency Turner did under the first Bush administration, and previously represented western New York in Congress for almost 20 years.

Kemp's first public role, however, was as a journeyman NFL quarterback in the 1950s and 1960s. He played for the Pittsburgh Steelers, Los Angeles Chargers and Buffalo Bills, among others, and also spent time in the Canadian Football League with the Calgary Stampeders.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell — whose father Charles Goodell represented Kemp’s area as a Republican in Congress in the 1960s — was quoted as calling Kemp an "extraordinary American leader who became a trusted colleague and exceptional friend to countless NFL owners, team personnel and commissioners after his MVP playing career with the Buffalo Bills."

Kemp, who died in 2009, said that professional football gave him a "good perspective" for politics.

"When I entered the political arena, I had already been booed, cheered, cut, sold, traded, and hung in effigy," he said, according to the Bills.

The only active member of Congress with an NFL history is Rep. Burgess Owens, a retiring Republican from Utah.

Owens, a former New York Jets safety, has alluded to his NFL career at times, largely focusing on criticizing the politicization of sports.

He previously told Fox Business during a time when players were kneeling for the national anthem that he would be boycotting games until Goodell was fired.

"I’m done," he told host David Asman in 2020. "It’s time for these young men who make millions of dollars to say thank you [and respect the country]."

Owens did not respond to a request for comment.

Former longtime Philadelphia Eagles offensive tackle Jon Runyan Sr. also parlayed his playing career into one on Capitol Hill.

The Republican represented part of South Jersey for two terms in a district now represented by Rep. Herb Conaway, D-N.J., that covers part of the Pine Barrens and Philadelphia suburbs.

Runyan is now a vice president of policy and rules with the NFL and his son Jon Jr. is a guard with the Giants. He did not respond to a request for comment.

Another NFC East player who went on to serve in Congress was former Rep. Heath Shuler, D-N.C.

Shuler, who played quarterback for the franchise now known as the Washington Commanders, parlayed his playing career into a congressional career in 2006 before being succeeded by Republican Mark Meadows, a later close ally of President Donald Trump.

Colin Allred, a former Tennessee Titan, also moved on to Congress, where he served until 2025.

This cycle, he unsuccessfully challenged state Rep. James Talarico and U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, for Sen. John Cornyn’s seat.

Cornyn lost his primary earlier this year to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton who now faces Talarico.

There have been several other top-name lawmakers who themselves were former professional athletes.

Rep. Anthony Gonzalez, an Indiana Republican who chose not to seek re-election in 2022 over political fallout from voting to impeach Trump, was a former Indianapolis Colts wide receiver.

Former Seattle Seahawks wide receiver Steve Largent — an NFL Hall of Famer — went on to represent Oklahoma in Congress.

Former Philadelphia Phillies pitcher Jim Bunning went on to have a lengthy political career.

He was elected to the Kentucky State Senate in 1979, Congress in 1986 and later the U.S. Senate in 1999.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., now holds his seat.

New York Knicks star Bill Bradley, whose number 24 has been retired in MSG, went on to serve New Jersey in the U.S. Senate as a Democrat in the 1980s and 90s.

He also mounted an unsuccessful presidential primary bid against former Sen. Al Gore, D-Tenn.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Ex-Nebraska Cornhuskers head coach Tom Osborne – who briefly played for the Redskins – also served his college’s home state in Congress in the early 2000s.

Former Rep. Adam Wyant, R-Pa., had a 10-year career in the early days of professional football. He played for the Greensburg Athletic Association in the 1890s.

Laverne Dilweg, an early Green Bay Packer, also represented Wisconsin in Congress as a Democrat in the 1920s and 30s.

Former Arizona Democratic Congressman Mo Udall — whose family is considered political royalty throughout much of the Mountain West — spent three decades in Congress after a brief stint with the Denver Nuggets.

Olympic gold medal-winning decathlete Bob Mathias returned to the United States after the Helsinki Games and represented California as a Republican for about a decade beginning in 1967.

item.title: Cajun Navy leader warns Nolan Wells' search area has deadly 'washing machine' currents: 'Lots of drownings'
item.description: A United Cajun Navy leader says the waters near Horn Island where Nolan Wells was found are known as a "washing machine" due to deadly rip currents.
item.content:encoded:
MISSISSIPPI – A United Cajun Navy leader who helped search for Nolan Wells says the water around where the teen was found is notorious for deadly "washing machine" currents, and water conditions the day he vanished were far from ideal.

Wells, 18, disappeared July 4 after a boat trip with friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast. A National Park Service ranger found his remains on the island's northwestern tip two days later, on July 6, after crews searched the area.

Wells' friends returned to the mainland that afternoon without him. Jackson County Sheriff John Ledbetter has said investigators believe Wells chose to stay on the island. It wasn't until later that night that his mother learned from one of Wells' friends that he was missing, and she reported it to authorities.

SEARCH CALLED OFF AFTER BODY MATCHING MISSING TEEN NOLAN WELLS FOUND OFF MISSISSIPPI COAST

The stretch of water between Horn Island, where Wells was found dead, and neighboring Ship Island is known to locals as a "washing machine" because of its deadly rip currents, United Cajun Navy Vice President Brian Trascher told Fox News Digital. Authorities previously told the Associated Press that foul play isn't suspected.

"Yeah, there is some kind of nickname for it, and it's because they've had a lot of drownings in that area and on that island. And to the west, there's Ship Island, just another few miles to the West. And in between those two islands, there's a strong divergent occurrence," Trascher said. "And that area is called the washing machine by locals."

Based on conversations with people who were on Horn Island on July 4, Trascher said the rip current that day was "extremely strong," adding that the water off the island's northwest tip can go from shallow to deep in just a few steps.

NOLAN WELLS' HOMETOWN OFFICIALS RALLY BEHIND SHERIFF AFTER 'DERELICT IN THEIR DUTIES' ATTACK

While Wells knew how to swim and swam regularly, Trascher said a strong rip current can overpower even an experienced swimmer, especially if panic, sun exposure or alcohol are factors.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Trascher said one of the biggest unresolved questions in Wells' death is what happened between when he was last seen, around 4 or 4:30 p.m. on July 4, and when his body was found, calling it a "gaping hole" that still needs to be answered.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"I've heard virtually no explanation, no eyewitness accounts. Nobody seemed to see him after that... there don't seem to be any photographs or videos of him after that time. So what happened? It wasn't dark yet. There was still a lot of people on the island... why did he just vanish and show up dead two days later?" Trascher said. "That is a question that needs to be asked. And I'm not suggesting that means that there was foul play involved. I'm just saying that there is a gaping hole in the story that needs to filled."

NOLAN WELLS INDEPENDENT AUTOPSY DOESN'T POINT TO FOUL PLAY, FORMER MEDICAL EXAMINER SAYS

During a Wednesday news conference, attorney Ben Crump revealed that an area of "red discoloration" was found on Wells' head, but said Dr. Roger Mitchell, who performed an independent autopsy, couldn't come to a conclusion on a cause or manner of death "pending further investigation." An official autopsy into Wells' death hasn't been completed.

SEND US A TIP

When asked by Fox News Digital about the case, forensic pathologist Dr. Michael Baden said the head injury doesn't point to foul play.

"So that could be from bumping into something in the water. There's a lot of debris in the water, for example. It depends how deep it is, but it's describing a really superficial impact that could have happened before death or after death," Baden said. "What he's describing is a minor injury that could be... totally innocent."

Without having additional information, Mitchell wrote in his report that he couldn't rule out the possibility that "non-accidental factors contributed to or caused the death."

item.title: Here's what you missed from Trump's first WHCA Dinner as president: 5 takeaways from his night with the press
item.description: Trump roasted Robert F. Kennedy, Kaitlan Collins, and Bari Weiss while sharing rare warm words for journalists at the historic dinner event.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump attended the annual White House Correspondents Association (WHCA) Dinner Friday night for the first time in either of his two presidential terms.

The event was rescheduled from its original April 25 date after a crazed gunman allegedly tried to assassinate the 47th president, bull rushing security with several weapons and firing a shot before he was taken into custody.

Here are five top highlights from the dinner:

TRUMP HEADS BACK TO CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER MONTHS AFTER GUNFIRE FORCED EVACUATION

Trump and the press typically find themselves at odds, and while Friday night had its share of uncomfortable moments, both sides were able to find some common ground — especially after sharing a scary moment at the originally scheduled dinner in April.

Before presenting one of the many awards of the night, ABC's Jon Karl thanked the president for his attendance.

"Mr. President, I want to say it matters that you came here tonight," said Karl. "For more than 100 years, presidents have chosen to sit in a room of reporters who asked tough and often uncomfortable questions, and who report without fear or favor. It's important. Thank you for being here."

TRUMP PRAISES PRESS AFTER WHCD SHOOTING, SAYS UNITY AT DINNER WAS 'BEAUTIFUL'

WHCA outgoing President and the dinner's emcee Weijia Jiang also had kind words for the president, just before she introduced him to speak and after discussing the importance of the First Amendment.

"President Trump, I've covered you for a long time, and so have many reporters in this room. When we ask questions, you push back, you give us answers and we push back," she said. "You have always been a deal guy. Well, that's the deal. And the First Amendment is a done deal. And that's what we toast tonight. The freedoms that brought us back together even after they were threatened." 

"So let's raise a glass to what makes ours a beautiful country."

Later in the night, Trump concluded his speech with a warm message for the press delivered in his own style.

JOURNALISTS DEMAND WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' ASSOCIATION 'SPEAK TRUTH TO POWER' IN NEW DINNER WITH TRUMP

"I just want to say, this room — I have tremendous respect for the people in this room," Trump said. 

"Sometimes I don’t feel you treat me fair, maybe you do, I don’t know," he continued. "I don’t feel that. But sometimes you treat me fairly, and I have a lot of respect for your profession. It’s amazing. And I just want to thank you for having me, and it’s been fun."

Trump made a series of jokes throughout his speech, some targeting the press, and others targeting people he appointed to positions of power.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was on the receiving end of a quip from the 47th president after Trump told attendees he hoped they enjoyed their beef tenderloin dinner.

"I want you all to know that Bobby Kennedy, who's right here, personally ran over the cow with his car," he jabbed. "And he cut it up and he brought it here for you to eat tonight."

Kennedy is well known for his eccentric history with animals, including once saying he captured a raccoon and cut its genitals off, viral videos of him catching dangerous snakes and once using a chainsaw to remove the head of a dead whale that washed up on Cape Cod.

"Bobby also suggested an appetizer featuring his favorite cut of male raccoon roadkill. But we drew the line at that," the president went on. "We said, 'No, we're not doing that.'"

Kennedy is also known for pushing a more red-meat centric diet and has embraced the push for restaurants to use beef tallow to fry their food instead of seed oils. 

Trump also joked about the shooting at the first WHCA dinner earlier this year, which pro-MAGA rapper Nikki Minaj attended.

"But after hearing the gunshots, many people yelled, ‘get down, get down!’ Which caused Nicki Minaj to start twerking, do you believe? Get down! She's the only one that really understood what that meant," Trump joked, earning laughter from the tough crowd.

Throughout his speech, he repeatedly used one of his famous phrases — referring to the press as "fake news," but took some direct shots at certain outlets and figures.

He unexpectedly flipped the script in a misdirection from what seemed like an update on the Iran war.

"A once feared and powerful regime that relentlessly attacked America has finally been toppled," he said. "Their former leaders have been removed and they’re now being run by a gay dictator facing internal divisions. But I, for one, wish Bari Weiss all the best at CBS News."

Trump's nemesis, Kaitlan Collins of CNN, was also on the receiving end of a brutal blow.

"I thought Kaitlan Collins had really made it big with a major new sponsorship, but then I informed her that it wasn't her on the Bud Light can, it was Dylan Mulvaney," he said, referencing the beer brand's failed marketing campaign featuring a transgender influencer.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, who is currently in the confirmation process to take on the job full-time, became part of mentalist Oz Pearlman's routine to close out the night.

In a convoluted bit, Oz asked Blanche to make up an amount of money he had in his wallet. Blanche said $130, but Oz guessed the correct amount — $85. Then, Oz asked a man sitting next to Blanche to choose a single bill from Blanche's wallet, and then had Blanche sign it. Blanche signed it, and was instructed to sit on it.

For the remainder of the act, Oz asked members of the crowd to stand — including Fox News' Kevin Corke — and dream up a person dead or alive who they wished they could interview. He guessed several of interview subjects' names correctly, and even enlisted the help of a member of the crowd, who also made correct guesses.

After that, he enlisted audience members, once of which was former National Security Administrator and current U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Watlz, to chose important dates and random numbers. When multiplied, those numbers equaled 53,670,682. 

Oz then turned back to Blanche and asked him to stand up and look at the serial number of the bill he was sitting on. Audience members were stunned to find out it was No. 53670682.

Trump explained that he was tired of asking his communications team, Karoline Leavitt and Steven Cheung, if he had received any calls from the press. So instead he started to give journalists his direct line, which has turned out to be a disaster.

"That was the stupidest thing I ever did," the president said. "I'm getting a call every 3.7 minutes."

"Every once in a while, it'll be one of the people in this room that I like and I'll pick it up," he said, referencing taking phone calls from Fox News' Jacqui Heinrich and joking that she only wants to discuss "horrible" subjects.

But he said that other callers are from outlets that he has never heard of or are just starting out. 

"You know, I pick up every once in a while, 'hello, I'm from Reno, Nevada. We're a startup paper. We're calling us the Reno Express,'" Trump continued. "I'll say, 'Do you believe it, I'm the president of the United States.'"

"'Mr. President, could I have your views on Iran?' And I just hang up," Trump continued. "No, I get the craziest calls. I mean, some of them. My wife said, I can't believe you do this. This is a hell of a way to live."

Trump had never attended the WHCA Dinner in either of his two presidencies, a total of five years, breaking with long-held tradition for a night of comradery with the press and government officials. His attendance Friday night was a major storyline — especially after the event in April was foiled by a lone gunman.

The president laid his plans for next year towards the conclusion of his hour-and-four-minute remarks.

"It's an honor to do it," Trump said of his attendance. "I've been to it numerous times, but as president, I haven't been here, and I'm glad."

Trump expects to attend again in 2027, but joked that his decision could depend on how the press behaves.

"They said, 'Would you do it next year?' I said, 'I will be back next year,'" Trump said. "Now if you get really, really nasty, maybe not. I don't know. But we're going to be back next year."

Trump attended the WHCA Dinner in 2011 and 2015, when he was a successful businessman, real estate tycoon and reality television personality.

item.title: Mace breaks with Trump, questions whether Lindsey Graham's sister is 'qualified' for ballot
item.description: Nancy Mace questions whether Darline Graham meets South Carolina ballot eligibility rules, citing new state laws on Republican primary voting.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., is questioning whether President Donald Trump's preferred candidate to succeed the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — his sister, Darline Graham — is even eligible to appear on South Carolina's Republican primary ballot.

"She has no record and I'm not even sure that she's qualified to be on the ballot," Mace told Fox News Digital.

Her comments come as Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., announced on Fox News that she will enter next month’s special primary election to run for a full term in the Senate.

DARLINE GRAHAM REVEALS WHAT TRUMP TOLD HER INSIDE OVAL OFFICE AFTER BROTHER LINDSEY'S DEATH

"Obviously I feel for her and losing Lindsey Graham — the entire state is mourning right now," Mace said of Graham.

"It's admirable and honorable what she's done to take the wings for the next six months, but she has no records and I am not even sure she's qualified to be on the ballot," she repeated.

Mace isn’t alone in her concerns over Graham’s qualifications to serve a full-term. Local South Carolina GOP Chairman CJ Westfall said in a statement that he is pursuing a formal determination of whether Graham meets the party’s qualifications to run.

He said the request followed conversations with local voters about Graham’s qualifications, including concerns over her lack of political experience and her voting record — concerns Mace shares.

"It's not clear that she's voted in enough Republican primary elections to be on the ballot," Mace said when asked why Graham may not be qualified.

MACE SNUBS TRUMP'S PREFERRED SENATE CANDIDATE, BACKS RALPH NORMAN INSTEAD

"By new state election laws of July of this year, you had to have voted in the last two of the last three Republican primaries and it's not clear she has."

Mace has instead chosen to endorse Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., for the Senate seat.

"He's a tried-and-true conservative," Mace said. "He doesn't bend, he does not back down, and he has a 100% conservative voting record.

"We have a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to get a conservative into the U.S. Senate in this seat. We're not going to have this opportunity again in a while."

REP RALPH NORMAN ENTERS SOUTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE DESPITE TRUMP'S ENDORSEMENT OF DARLINE GRAHAM

Mace herself was widely considered a likely candidate to enter the race for the South Carolina Senate seat, but she announced Monday that she would not run.

Trump, regardless of any doubts of qualifications, threw in his endorsement for Graham to seek a full-term seat, posting to Truth Social after a White House meeting with her, "run, Darline, run."

While Trump’s endorsements have oftentimes been the winners of their respective primaries, Mace isn’t sold on the idea that Trump’s pick will influence South Carolina voters heavily.

"I think that you'll see that South Carolina voters seem to be a little more… they're conservative, but they're also independent," Mace said. "Independent conservatives."

"They vote the way that they wanna vote, not because someone told them to. And I think you'll see that in this race."

item.title: Meghan Markle's 'MasterChef Australia' controversy may be exactly the point: experts
item.description: Meghan Markle's "MasterChef Australia" guest judge role sparks boycott calls and praise as royal experts debate whether the appearance can reset her brand.
item.content:encoded:
Meghan Markle's upcoming appearance on "MasterChef Australia" has already sparked debate, with royal experts telling Fox News Digital the backlash may be just as important as the episode itself.

The hit reality cooking series announced in an Instagram post that the 44-year-old Duchess of Sussex would be joining the show as a guest judge for Sunday's episode, writing that Markle will be "bringing her love of food, entertaining and seasonal produce to one of the competition's most memorable challenges."

In a press release, Markle, who filmed the episode during her visit to Australia with her husband Prince Harry in April, explained why she wanted to take part in the episode.

'MASTERCHEF' FINALIST SAYS BUSY FAMILIES ARE LOSING SOMETHING MORE IMPORTANT THAN HOME-COOKED MEALS

"What attracted me to the MasterChef Australia kitchen? Two things: my love of food and my love of Australia. It was an easy yes," Markle said.

"It’s such a great show," she continued. "I’m just really honored that I was asked to be able to be here with you and to be able to judge some of these meals."

The press release noted that the cooks will take on the challenge of creating "a dish fit for a Duchess" using some of Markle's "favorite seasonal ingredients."

MEGHAN MARKLE'S SHOW EMMY NOMINATION 'SOMEWHAT BAFFLING' DUE TO LACKLUSTER RATINGS: EXPERT

In a preview of the episode that appeared on Sydney's 10 News, Markle appeared alongside season 18 "MasterChef Australia" judges Poh Ling Yeow, Sofia Levin and Jean-Christophe Novelli.

Markle introduced her chosen ingredients, noting that the chefs had "quite the bounty her" and proudly sharing that her children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, "eat Brussels sprouts."

"That’s impressive," Levin said.

PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE’S HOLLYWOOD DREAMS HIT WALL AS EXPERT WARNS OF ‘TOXIC BRAND’ STIGMA

"Food and cooking to me is really a love language," Markle explained later in the preview. "I think it’s such a great way to connect. It’s something that can feel sentimental and meaningful and It’s how I, it’s how I show my nurturing and love for my friends, family, and my kids."

Following the announcement, Markle's participation in "MasterChef Australia" was quickly met with a divided reaction on social media, earning both praise from supporters and calls for a boycott from critics.

"Why? She’s not a chef??? Not interested!" one Instagram user wrote.

"Can't stand her. She's not a chef," another agreed, adding, "Why is she even on this show."

"Thanks for the heads-up and making it easier to avoid," one critic commented as another chimed in, "Definitely won't watch it!"

"First time since the beginning of this show, that I WON’T be watching, first time!!" another detractor wrote.

However, others expressed their excitement over seeing Markle's appearance.

"Can’t wait to watch it!!!" one social media user commented.

"I'll be WATCHING!!" another added.

"I know she will do a great job," a fan enthused.

"I CAN'T WAIT!! WE LOVE YOU PRINCESS MEGHAN," another supporter wrote.

"I love this for her… she is working and finding opportunities for herself," one fan added.

"All the people saying they won’t watch are the first ones who will be watching and later criticizing," another commenter wrote. "I can’t wait to watch! Love Meghan!"

Markle's appearance also made headlines and fueled debate online after a report claimed her team requested that she not be referred to as "royalty" during filming.

The polarized reaction to Markle's latest gig underscores a familiar pattern for the Duchess of Sussex, whose post-royal ventures have often generated as much controversy as publicity.

Royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital the attention surrounding Markle's appearance, whether positive or negative, could ultimately benefit both the duchess and the cooking competition.

"Every time Meghan’s name gets in the papers, even if it is negative, it builds up the power of her brand," he said. "It also helps to hype the show before it starts."

"She was chosen as a guest judge to boost the ratings of the show," Fitzwilliams added.

While Markle's role has prompted questions about her qualifications, British broadcaster Helena Chard argued that professional cooking experience isn't necessarily a requirement for a celebrity guest judge.

"I don’t believe she’s a qualified chef. But then, they’ve had Steve Irwin as a guest judge before and he wasn’t a chef either," she pointed out. "So it’s not really about culinary credentials."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

The "Suits" alum's guest judging stint marks her latest foray into the food and lifestyle world. In March 2025, Markle's "With Love, Meghan" lifestyle and reality show premiered on Netflix. In the show, Meghan shared cooking, gardening and entertaining tips alongside celebrity guests. "With Love, Meghan" also served as a launchpad for her As Ever lifestyle brand.

In January 2026, Netflix reportedly canceled the show after two seasons and later announced that it was ending its partnership with the As Ever brand though Markle and Prince Harry retained a first-look production deal with the streamer. However, "With Love, Meghan" recently received a surprise Daytime Emmy Award nomination for outstanding lifestyle series. "Meghan does have an interest in food and entertaining," Chard noted. "So from a PR perspective, appearing on ‘MasterChef Australia’ alongside well-known hosts, strengthens her brand."

While Chard saw the guest judging role as a natural fit, other royal experts told Fox News Digital that the response illustrates the challenges Markle continues to face with public perception after stepping away from royal life.

"People are talking more about why she's judging than what she's judging," royal reporter Kinsey Schofield said. "An image reset only works if the audience buys into the new image, and right now many viewers still see a disconnect between Meghan's branding and her actual experience or authority in this space."

"Social media always amplifies the loudest voices," the "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered" host continued. "That said, there does seem to be a broader sense of Meghan fatigue. Every project arrives carrying years of baggage, and that's a challenge most celebrities simply don't have. She isn't launching from a blank slate. She's launching from a very divided public reputation."

Fitzwilliams agreed, saying there have been "sufferers from Meghan fatigue for some time" and that "a great many viewers feel this way."

"Lifestyle is aspirational, it's lucrative, and it gives celebrities tremendous control over their image," Schofield said. "The problem is that audiences don't just buy recipes or table settings anymore. They're buying authenticity."

Fitzwilliams shared his view that Markle's cameo is also tied to her broader business ambitions. "She is returning to food in the hope this boosts sales of the As Ever products," he said.

Schofield said that the guest judge appearance may not deliver the hoped-for results, arguing that every project that Markle takes on is now judged through the lens of the duchess herself.

"Meghan has had several opportunities to reinvent herself since leaving royal life, and the pattern has remained the same… enormous publicity followed by polarized reactions," she told Fox News Digital. "One television appearance probably won't rewrite that narrative overnight."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"People often react to the brand before they react to the product," she added. "That's the downside of building such a personality-driven business model. Every project becomes less about the content itself and more about whether people have bought into Meghan as the person selling it."

Beyond the public reaction, some royal experts questioned whether audiences would view her as a credible choice to critique contestants on "MasterChef Australia."

"Celebrity guest judges aren't expected to have Michelin stars, but they do need to bring something credible to the table," Schofield said. "Meghan's challenge is that she's still trying to establish herself as an authority in this space while much of the audience sees her as someone playing a part."

Royal expert Hilary Fordwich shared her opinion that Markle's divisive public image makes her guest appearance different from most casting decisions.

"Meghan is so polarizing that while such an appearance would be low-risk for any regular celebrity, it is likely to backfire," she said, adding that the duchess "has no credentials" and "doesn't come across as authentic."

"Given the failure of her previous cooking attempts, with lackluster ratings, this is all she can do now which is to be involved in a show which is already a success," Fordwich said.

However, royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner shared a more optimistic outlook on Markle's latest endeavor.

"Meghan is a master at reinventions, keeping herself in the public eye, and ‘MasterChef Australia’ is the latest platform to succumb to the real values of the lady and obviously cooking is one of many talents," he said.

Turner pointed to Markle's previous charitable work with the Hubb Community Kitchen, which was established in the wake of London's devastating Grenfell Tower fire. In June 2017, a fire ignited in the 24-story Grenfell Tower apartment block which killed 72 people and displaced hundreds of residents. After becoming involved with the community kitchen in 2018, Markle cooked alongside local women and helped publish a charity cookbook that raised money to support the initiative.

The royal expert told Fox News Digital that he also believed Markle would resonate with Australian audiences.

"Australia is a country which values people who have initiative and drive, and Meghan has that people's touch to support and offer cookery as one of her skill bases," he said.

For all the debate surrounding Markle's guest judging role, experts said the real question is whether the attention translates into viewers.

Schofield believes Markle's appearance could prove beneficial for "MasterChef Australia" if the buzz prompts audiences to tune in.

"Meghan guarantees headlines, and headlines translate into curiosity," she said. "Whether that curiosity becomes ratings or resentment is the million-dollar question. Producers know controversy can be good for television, but only if viewers stay for the episode instead of switching it off."

item.title: Sophie Cunningham gets support from GOP senator after backlash over transgender sports comments
item.description: Sen. Darline Graham praised Sophie Cunningham's stance on transgender athletes in women's sports, calling it dangerous to have boys in girls' sports.
item.content:encoded:
Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham received support Friday from Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., after the WNBA player doubled down this week on her comments that it is "common sense" to keep biological males out of women's sports.

In a statement released Friday, Graham thanked Cunningham for speaking publicly on the issue.

"I want to thank Sophie Cunningham for speaking out and make it clear that I could not agree more," Graham said.

WHITE HOUSE DEFENDS WNBA STAR SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM AFTER SHE SPEAKS OUT IN SUPPORT OF PROTECTING WOMEN'S SPORTS

"What she said took a lot of guts. It's sad but true that in today's world, and particularly on this issue, common sense is not common."

Graham, who described herself as a "volleyball mom," said she knows "how dangerous it is to have boys playing in girls' sports" after years of traveling with her daughter's team throughout South Carolina and the Southeast.

She also referenced a North Carolina high school volleyball player who was seriously injured after being struck by a hit from a transgender athlete.

US MASTERS SWIMMING COMPETITOR SAYS HER GRIEVANCE FOR TRANS ATHLETE COMMENTS HAS BEEN RESOLVED

"As a mother, thank you to Miss Cunningham for speaking out," Graham said. "I truly appreciate you adding your voice to this important debate. Our daughters will be the ones who benefit from your words and voice."

Cunningham reiterated her position Wednesday before the Fever's 123-88 victory over the Connecticut Sun after first making the remarks in an ESPN profile earlier this week.

"I said what I said. I think it's kind of common sense," Cunningham told reporters. "And I think I'll always believe in that. I think it's really important to protect children, and that's little girls who are also involved in that category. I stand on what I said."

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM DOUBLES DOWN AHEAD OF SUN GAME AFTER ESPN PROFILE STIRS CONTROVERSY: 'I SAID WHAT I SAID'

Cunningham also said she believes protecting women's sports is consistent with the intent of Title IX and maintained that her comments were not directed against transgender people.

"But I'm also there to love biological women, and I think that there are rights that need to be protected," Cunningham said. "And, like I said, I'm gonna stand true to that. I'll never falter in my beliefs in that. But I have never once stated that I hated the trans community."

The Indiana Fever later released a statement saying Cunningham's views are her own.

"Our players are thoughtful adults with their own perspectives and voices, and those views are their own," the team said. "We are committed to welcoming fans from every background and treating everyone with respect, and that's what guides us as an organization."

The debate over transgender athletes in girls' and women's sports has become a major issue in recent years. President Donald Trump signed an executive order in 2025 aimed at barring transgender athletes from competing in girls' and women's sports, while the Supreme Court recently allowed state laws restricting transgender athletes' participation to remain in effect as legal challenges continue.

item.title: 8 family members, including 6 children, found dead in Michigan fire; at least one victim shot: police
item.description: At least some of the eight victims found inside the burning Grand Haven Township home had been shot, prompting a suspicious death investigation.
item.content:encoded:
Authorities in Michigan are investigating possible foul play after eight people, including six children, were found dead inside a burning home Friday with some of the victims suffering gunshot wounds.

The Ottawa County Sheriff's Office launched a suspicious death investigation after responding to a house fire in Grand Haven Township and discovering multiple fatalities.

Authorities said the victims—all believed to be related—include six children between the ages of 5 and 15 and two adults in their 40s.

TWO TEEN SUSPECTS HELD AFTER 5 FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN 'TARGETED MASS SHOOTING'

Investigators believe all eight lived at the home and are working to formally identify them.

The Grand Haven Fire Department initially responded to reports of the smell of smoke in the area between 8:30 a.m. and 9 a.m. on Friday, but firefighters were unable to locate a fire.

Just before 11:45 a.m., deputies and firefighters returned after receiving reports of white smoke coming from a home in the 14900 block of Riverside Trail.

FAMILY IDENTIFIES YOUNG WOMAN FOUND FATALLY SHOT IN HOME OWNED BY REP AYANNA PRESSLEY'S HUSBAND

After extinguishing the fire, emergency crews discovered the eight victims inside the residence.

The sheriff's office said investigators later determined that at least some of the victims had been shot.

Authorities said the investigation remains active and additional information is expected following the completion of the victims' autopsies.

Sheriff's detectives are investigating alongside arson investigators with the Michigan State Police.

item.title: After Platner implosion, Maine Democrats rush toward new Senate nominee despite fresh warning signs
item.description: The Maine Senate race is rated a toss-up as Troy Jackson runs on Medicare for all and abolishing ICE against Republican incumbent Susan Collins.
item.content:encoded:
BANGOR, Maine - The sprint to replace ex-candidate Graham Platner will come to an end on Saturday as Maine Democrats are expected to quickly elevate Troy Jackson as their party's nominee in the high-stakes Senate showdown with longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins.

Jackson, a former state Senate president, is on a glide path to replace Platner at the Maine Democratic Party nominating convention in Bangor, after winning the vast majority of the voting delegates chosen last weekend by Democrats in the northern New England state's 16 counties. And Jackson's top rivals in the race to replace Platner backed him after dropping out of the race the past few days, leaving only one long-shot candidate for delegates to also consider at the convention.

The Senate race in Maine, where Collins is the only GOP incumbent running for re-election in a state President Donald Trump lost in the 2024 election, is one of roughly a dozen midterm showdowns across the country that will determine if Republicans hold onto their slim majority or if the Democrats win back control of the chamber.

"Let’s get to work to defeat Susan Collins and create the Maine that working people deserve," Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from the remote northern tip of Maine and a one-time conservative Republican who became a Democrat over two decades ago, said in a social media post ahead of the convention.

WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN: CHECK OUT THE FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS ON THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS

While Jackson quickly raised over $1 million for his burgeoning Senate campaign and coalesced party support, there are some potential warning signs.

Following reports this past week digging into Jackson's alleged temper and workplace conduct, reported claims of mortgage improprieties as well as other potential liabilities including his past strict anti-abortion stance, there are concerns by some in the party that following the Platner implosion, Democrats have landed another unvetted nominee.

"This is a bit of a rocket vetting process," a Democratic strategist who works on Senate races, who asked to remain anonymous to speak more freely, told Fox News Digital. "Maine Democrats have seemingly made their choice and they're just going to have to ride with it."

A veteran Democratic consultant who also asked for anonymity said that "it's very clear that Democrats should not be looking to Maine to flip the Senate"

"The good news is that we have upset opportunities in places like Texas, Iowa, and Alaska," added the consultant, who works with centrist Democratic Senate candidates.

Platner, a military combat veteran and oyster farmer who was backed progressive champion and Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont soon after he launched his bid last August, saw his campaign quickly catch fire. Two-term Democratic Gov. Janet Mills, who was heavily recruited by longtime Democratic Senate leader Sen. Chuck Schumer to run for the Senate, suspended her campaign this spring after trailing Platner in fundraising and in the polls.

FIVE THINGS TO KNOW ABOUT TROY JACKSON, WHO'S ABOUT TO REPLACE GRAHAM PLATNER AS THE DEMOCRATS' SENATE NOMINEE

But even as Platner steamrolled the Democratic establishment and crushed the competition last month in Maine's primary to capture the nomination, he had already been forced on defense in the wake of a slew of scandals.

Platner dropped out earlier this month, amid calls from top Democrats in Maine and across the country to immediately exit the race following an explosive report containing an allegation of rape from a woman he previously dated. Platner denied the report but stepped aside.

Jackson, who unsuccessfully ran for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, campaigned alongside Platner during the primary. And he quickly made the case that he was the best equipped candidate to grab the mantle of the progressive and populist movement that had backed Platner.

Similar to Platner, Jackson is running on a platform aimed at working-class voters. He backs raising taxes on billionaires, the universal healthcare system known as "Medicare-for-all," abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and he opposes military aid to Israel at a time that Democrats are increasingly divided on support for America's longtime Middle East ally.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Jackson, who also had Sanders' support as he ran governor, is currently backed in his Senate campaign by Our Revolution, the group born in 2016 out of Sanders' first presidential campaign.

Rep. Ro Khanna of California, a leading progressive in the House and a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, was a top Platner backer. Khanna quickly moved his support to Jackson in this month's sprint to succeed Platner.

And Jackson enjoys strong support from labor unions in Maine. The labor backing, along with support from Platner’s former allies, helped Jackson capture the overwhelming majority of county-selected delegates last weekend.

The 500 delegates chosen last weekend, along with 101 selected by the state party, will vote for the nominee at the convention. While the delegates on Jackson's slate are not required to support him at the convention, he is considered all but certain to secure the nomination.

Republicans are arguing that Democrats stacked the deck to back Jackson as Platner's replacement.

"Maine voters have been shut out by the Democrat establishment with a rigged nominating process to crown Platner 2.0 without a single vote being cast," Republican National Committee spokesperson Kristen Cianci charged in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Collins, as she runs for a sixth six-year term in the Senate, is facing a rough political climate for Republicans, amid GOP President Donald Trump's underwater approval ratings, persistent inflation and what polls indicate is an unpopular war with Iran.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The senator, known as a moderate Republican who at times has voted against Trump, last month received bipartisan praise after reaching a milestone by casting her 10,000th consecutive Senate vote.

But Democrats are taking aim at Collins over her comments that she didn't regret her 2018 vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, despite his crucial vote four years later to overturn the landmark Roe v. Wade abortion ruling.

And following the fatal shooting in Maine earlier this month involving federal immigration agents, Democrats heavily criticized the Senate Appropriations Committee chair for her support for ICE funding.

But Collins has a history of defeating the Democrats' efforts to oust her from the Senate.

Six years ago, she trailed Democratic challenger Sara Gideon, the then-Maine House speaker, but the senator ended up winning re-election by nearly 9 points.

The Senate showdown in Maine is expected to be competitive, combustible, and expensive, with outside groups on both sides spending big bucks to run ads.

The first Fox News Power Rankings of the 2026 midterms, which gauge the competitiveness of elections using data, reporting and analysis, were released this week. And they rank the showdown in Maine as a toss-up.

Meanwhile, a Pine Tree Poll conducted in recent days by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center indicated Jackson with a slight three-point edge over Collins, right at the edge of the margin of error, among likely general election voters in Maine.

item.title: Democrats concede NJ voter-roll failure was ‘horrible’ — but reject broader fraud fears
item.description: Democratic lawmakers say New Jersey's motor vehicle system error registering 6,600 noncitizens demands accountability but reject widespread fraud claims.
item.content:encoded:
Democratic lawmakers told Fox News Digital they agree New Jersey's voter registration error demands accountability but say it doesn't justify claims of widespread election fraud.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Tuesday said a "serious software error" led to the mistaken registration of roughly 6,600 noncitizens through the state's Motor Vehicle System, while the company that provides the identity-related security services denied any wrongdoing.

"In New Jersey, we absolutely need to have accountability for what happened," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said.

"It was just horrible. There was a big problem with that computer problem that they had. We need to try to address that going forward."

NEW JERSEY REMOVES 6,600 PEOPLE FROM VOTER ROLLS WHO WERE ELIGIBLE TO CAST A BALLOT FOR 2024 ELECTION

Kim said states should be given the tools to keep voter rolls accurate instead of relying on the Department of Homeland Security's findings after the agency found roughly 250,000 potential noncitizens who may be registered to vote across New Jersey, California, Nevada and Pennsylvania during a preliminary review.

"The main thing is making sure states have what they need," Kim added. "I don't trust the idea that we're just going to mesh it with some DHS database. That's where a lot of the problems come in, but we should all be making sure we're looking out for election integrity."

Sherrill said she immediately ordered an investigation after the error was discovered and that the state's Division of Elections is removing ineligible voters from the rolls. She said fewer than 400 of those improperly registered cast ballots.

Kim said improving election technology and maintaining paper trails need to be a priority.

GOP ERUPTS OVER 6,600 NONCITIZEN VOTERS FOUND IN BLUE STATE AS SCANDAL DEEPENS: ‘WORSE THAN ANYONE EXPECTED’

"I've been pushing on that. Why don't we get behind that?" he said.

Pointing to state and county officials, Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, said they must ensure "only those who are eligible to vote, vote."

The comments also come after House Democrats largely opposed a legislative package combining a congressional stock trading ban with federal voter ID measures, as New Jersey's voter registration error reignites debate.

When asked whether the country needs a nationwide proof-of-citizenship requirement for voting, Rep. Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y., said President Donald Trump's claims of widespread election fraud are "a figment of his imagination."

"There's no evidence for it, and I'm not going to validate his false narratives," he said.

Despite acknowledging those involved should be "held accountable," Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., said noncitizen voting "remains extremely rare."

"I have always said that people should have to prove that they are who they say they are before they vote, and we have systems in place to ensure that happens, which is why noncitizen voting remains extremely rare," he said.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said the error was "not acceptable" and pointed to Virginia's voter ID requirements and election audits, saying they have never uncovered a noncitizen voting problem.

"We do have an ID requirement in Virginia," he said. "We also have audits of elections, and we've never found there to be a noncitizen voting problem."

Praising Sherrill for coming forward in a "transparent manner," Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., said election software should be continuously reviewed.

CALIFORNIA ACCUSED OF BLOCKING FEDERAL VOTER ROLL AUDIT AS DOJ ESCALATES PROBE OF ELECTION FRAUD CLAIMS

"We need to constantly be looking at election software and making sure," she said.

Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I., said he supports a "simple" voter ID law but opposed the House GOP bill because he said it went beyond a basic ID requirement.

"If they put up a simple voter ID bill for an up-or-down vote without any of the other bulls--- in it, I would vote for it," he said. "I think a lot of people on both sides would, too. But they keep adding other stuff, like gutting mail ballots, and that was the problem with yesterday's bill."

item.title: Azzi Fudd wins WNBA 3-point contest, becomes first rookie champion
item.description: Azzi Fudd made WNBA history as the first rookie to win the All-Star 3-point contest, scoring 30 of 40 possible points in the final round.
item.content:encoded:
Azzi Fudd put on a historic shooting display during her first WNBA All-Star weekend. The Dallas Wings guard won Friday night’s 3-point contest, becoming the first rookie in league history to win the event.

Fudd finished the first round with 30 points, 10 shy of the maximum possible score. Portland Fire star Bridget Carleton was eliminated after scoring 19 in the round. Fudd took 27 shots, missing just six of her attempts en route to winning the coveted title.

Fudd acknowledged she experienced some nerves Friday night. "You saw ‘only’ six shots, but I feel like that was a lot," Fudd said. "But honestly, I was really nervous. I was excited."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Fudd added: "It's fun to do because... and I don't want to sound cocky... but it's easy to me, just the set shot. Take the ball from the rack; it really is muscle memory. It's what I've been doing since I was young."

Fudd entered the All-Star break averaging 2.2 shots from beyond the 3-point arc this season. She's knocked down 53 total 3-pointers so far during her rookie year.

LIBERTY'S SABRINA IONESCU ADDRESSES ABSENCE FROM WNBA 3-POINT CONTEST: 'NEVER OFFICIALLY GOT INVITED'

While injuries impacted Fudd's college basketball career, Dallas valued her overall talent and took her with the first selection in April's WNBA Draft.

Fudd also said her injury setbacks came with an unexpected benefit. The repetitive shooting she did during rehab helped sharpen her form and build the rhythm needed to knock down shots from the same spots in Friday’s 3-point contest.

"That was a lot of chair shooting, a lot of stationary shots, so you get really good at shooting off of a rack and being stationary and robotic and having to knock your shot down."

Before the 3-point contest, the WNBA debuted another All-Star event in Chicago — the Shooting Stars competition.

Replacing the past skills challenge, the Shooting Stars competition featured four three-person teams. Each roster included one former player designated as a legend, one current player and one rising young player. Team Washington defeated Team Seattle to win the inaugural event.

item.title: Trump spares no one at WHCA dinner, taking aim at Dems, press and his own Cabinet
item.description: Trump scrapped his combative speech for a unity-themed address, but still took familiar jabs at J.B. Pritzker, Chuck Schumer, and Gavin Newsom.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump struck a more conciliatory tone Friday at the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner, scrapping the combative speech he had prepared before an assassination attempt upended the annual event in April. The rewrite emphasized unity and gratitude, though the president still couldn't resist slipping in a few familiar jabs at the press while insisting: "The show must go on."

Trump returned to the stage just months after gunfire abruptly ended the organization’s annual banquet. An armed suspect, Cole Allen, stormed the event in what authorities say was an attempt to assassinate the president.

"The speech that I had ready just a short while. Oh, that was going to be a doozy. I was so psyched. I was going to rip people. And I don't know, just something changed it — really for the better. But I just wouldn't want to do that," Trump said to a room full of journalists and government officials.

"But we'll do a little ripping, if you don't mind. But it is true. I said, how do we handle this is going to be a different kind of evening. And it is. And in many ways it's a more beautiful evening, actually," he added.

TRUMP HEADS BACK TO CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER MONTHS AFTER GUNFIRE FORCED EVACUATION

Trump teed up his typical walk-out song — Lee Greenwood's "God Bless the U.S.A." — and quickly jumped into joking about seeking a third term before striking a more serious chord as he thanked the Secret Service for its work, not only during the attack at the original Correspondents' Dinner, but for protecting him every day.

He delivered a speech that went longer than expected, talking for an hour and four minutes.

"Just like my presidency, the second time is always better. It's always better, and the third time will be better yet. I'm only kidding," Trump said to some chuckles throughout the room. 

The president said he could not deliver the same speech he had planned for the first dinner, "ripping" the press, but said "it was for the better" that he changed his remarks for the second time around.

COLE ALLEN INDICTED BY GRAND JURY ON FOUR CHARGES RELATED TO ALLEGED TRUMP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT

He made various jokes aimed at not just Democrats but his own cabinet members.

"I hope that everyone finally got to enjoy their entire very delicious beef tenderloins, very special beef. And I want you all to know that Bobby Kennedy, who's right here personally, ran over the cow and his car," said Trump.

TRUMP HEADS BACK TO CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER MONTHS AFTER GUNFIRE FORCED EVACUATION

He took aim at California Governor Gavin Newsom, former vice president Kamala Harris, possible 2028 presidential candidate Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker among other Democratic lawmakers and candidates.

" You can't have somebody like a J.B. Pritzker who I understand is not president, sadly. But, you know, some people say never used a fat word. And I know I would never call anybody fat," said Trump.

"I have my own problems, you know, it's not like I'm perfect, sir. In the back. Don't call him a fat pig, okay? That's. I'm sticking up for him. Don't call him you. You can't do that, sir. You can't call J.B. Pritzker a fat pig," said Trump.

Trump mocked Chuck Schumer's criticism of Israel and his increasingly vocal positions on the Israel-Hamas war.

"I'm going to send him a beautiful Palestinian outfit tomorrow so he can greet Bibi Netanyahu when he comes to town next week," joked Trump.

He used the moment to call for term limits, saying, "all joking aside, I do think we need term limits in Congress."

"The other day, a senator I knew got a text... 'When you get home, I want to have you immediately come up the stairs and make love to me.' And he said, 'I can't do both," joked Trump, saying that he can't both walk upstairs and have sex—he only has enough energy for one of those activities.

The WHCA honored U.S. Secret Service Officer Victor Gonzales during Friday's dinner in recognition of his actions in helping stop Allen from entering the ballroom.

The computer scientist from Torrance, California, traveled from Los Angeles to Washington, D.C. by Amtrak after purchasing a one-way ticket. Court filings say he sent a manifesto to family and friends shortly before the attack, describing political motivations and apologizing for his actions.

Allen has pleaded not guilty to charges including attempting to assassinate the president, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, transporting a firearm across state lines and assaulting a federal officer with a deadly weapon.

"The attempted mass murder at the Washington Hilton, that's what it could have been, was an assault on our democracy itself," Trump said in his speech, which spanned from jabs at Democrats, the press and some jokes at the expense of his own Cabinet.

PHOTO OF TRUMP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT SUSPECT COLE ALLEN IN HOTEL ROOM RELEASED AS DOJ SEEKS TO KEEP HIM JAILED

"One officer placed himself directly in harm's way and engaged the armed suspect, even after gunfire struck his protective vest. He stayed in the fight and the attacker was stopped," said Weijia Jiang, former WHCA president presenting the award to Gonzales.

"I know many of us have wondered. What if he hadn't acted in that exact way? What if he had waited a few more seconds? His courage that night reflects the core values of Secret Service duty, justice, courage, honesty and loyalty, and as a commitment to safeguarding his country and community," said Jiang.

During the speech, Trump highlighted his White House Ballroom following heat for the $200 million project, pointing to the lawsuits.

FIRST ON FOX: WHITE HOUSE REVEALS WHO’S JOINING TRUMP AT CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER — AND WHO CAN’T ATTEND

"In light of what we went through, I think, people understand it. It's going to be amazing, a phenomenal one of the biggest drone ports anywhere in the world," Trump said, referencing gunfire at the first WHCA Dinner.

Trump said that he "predicts" the WHCA would use the space for future dinners.

He also vowed to attend next year’s WHCA dinner.

"They said, 'Would you do it next year?' I said, 'I will be back next year,'" Trump said. "Now, if you get really, really nasty, maybe not. I don't know. But we're going to be back next year."

In his closing remarks, Trump said he has a "scoop" for the press announcing he is running for the fourth time.

He put on a red "TRUMP 2028" hat.

item.title: Gretchen Whitmer endorses moderate Haley Stevens in tight upcoming Senate primary
item.description: Gretchen Whitmer backed Haley Stevens over Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate primary as early voting begins, setting up a key Democratic clash.
item.content:encoded:
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer on Friday endorsed Rep. Haley Stevens ahead of the state’s U.S. Senate Democratic primary.

Stevens, a more centrist candidate, and progressive Dr. Abdul El-Sayed are considered the front-runners in the race as early voting starts on Saturday.

Whitmer’s endorsement could give Stevens a boost in a state where the governor twice won by considerable margins.

DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN

The governor also beat El-Sayed in the Democratic primary for governor in 2018.

Whitmer told supporters at a Teamsters hall in Detroit on Friday that Stevens has "what it takes to win" while appearing with her and South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn.

"Michiganders need a fighter in Washington and there are few leaders with more fight in ’em than Haley Stevens," Whitmer said at the event.

SWING-STATE POLL SPELLS TROUBLE FOR FAR LEFT AS SCHUMER-BACKED CANDIDATE DOMINATES WITH CRITICAL VOTING BLOCS

Stevens, who flipped a Republican House seat in 2018, is also backed by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Michigan Sen. Gary Peters, a two-term Democrat who is retiring from the seat.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt, and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are backing El-Sayed.

"The corporate establishment has closed ranks and made their pick – now, Michigan voters will get to make theirs," Roxie Richner, a spokesperson for El-Sayed, told the Associated Press.

JEWISH MICHIGAN DEMOCRATS ADMIT THEY WILL VOTE REPUBLICAN IF ABDUL EL-SAYED BECOMES NOMINEE

Michigan’s Democratic primary is on Aug. 4 and the winner will face Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers in November.

Democrats want to flip the U.S. Senate from narrow Republican control and must hold Michigan to do so.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Trump orders signs outside Smithsonian museum amid row over its depiction of American history
item.description: Trump's executive order targets federal sidewalks outside the Smithsonian to post signs directing visitors to a White House report on the museum.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump on Friday ordered his administration to install signs outside the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History directing visitors to what the White House describes as "accurate" information about the nation's past.

The executive order instructs the National Park Service, which maintains the sidewalks outside the museum, to place signs informing visitors about a White House report released July 4 that criticized the Smithsonian's portrayal of American history. Trump also directed the creation of a temporary exhibit intended to correct what his administration considers inaccurate historical information.

TRUMP WHITE HOUSE CALLS OUT SMITHSONIAN FOR PUSHING ‘ONE-SIDED, DIVISIVE POLITICAL NARRATIVES’

The move follows a report from Trump's Domestic Policy Council that accused the Smithsonian and the National Museum of American History of failing to present history "in a way that is inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic."

Because the Smithsonian operates independently of the executive branch, Trump cannot directly remove museum leadership or unilaterally change exhibits. Instead, the order targets federal property outside the museum that falls under National Park Service jurisdiction.

National Museum of American History Director Anthea M. Hartig defended the museum during congressional testimony this week.

"As we continue to fact check the report, we unwaveringly attest that it does not fairly or accurately characterize the full body of work at the museum," Hartig told lawmakers. "There is always room for improvement. But I also know the beauty and the inspiration and the expertise that lies in our collections, our exhibits, and our programming."

MED SCHOOL DEANS COME UP EMPTY IN TENSE HEARING WHEN ASKED POINT BLANK IF MEN CAN HAVE BABIES: 'RIDICULOUS'

Friday's order builds on Trump's broader effort to reshape the Smithsonian's exhibits.

In March, Trump signed an executive order directing the Smithsonian's Board of Regents to eliminate what the administration described as "improper, divisive or anti-American ideology" from the institution's museums.

The White House later criticized the National Museum of American History's "Entertainment Nation" exhibit, arguing displays about American pop culture framed the nation's history through an ideological lens rather than celebrating its achievements. White House official Lindsey Halligan previously told Fox News Digital that "American taxpayers should not be funding institutions that undermine our country or promote one-sided, divisive political narratives."

OBAMA JUDGE RULES ON EFFORT TO BLOCK AMERICA 250 EVENTS AT WH AND LINCOLN MEMORIAL

At the time, the Smithsonian said it was conducting a review of museum content and remained committed to "continuous and rigorous scholarship and research and unbiased presentation of facts and history."

The Smithsonian is overseen by a Board of Regents that includes Vice President JD Vance, Chief Justice John Roberts, members of Congress and citizen regents. The institution receives roughly two-thirds of its approximately $1 billion annual budget through federal appropriations.

Fox News Digital's Jasmine Baehr contributed to this report.

item.title: Fired '60 Minutes' correspondent accuses CBS News leadership of meddling in reporting
item.description: Cecilia Vega alleges CBS News meddled in her "60 Minutes" reporting on anti-ICE unrest and Trump's Iran war, calling directives "misinformation."
item.content:encoded:
Ousted "60 Minutes" correspondent Cecilia Vega spoke out against her former bosses at CBS News, alleging they had meddled in the show's reporting.

Vega, who was fired by the network in May, appeared Thursday at the National Association of Hispanic Journalists Conference & Expo in New Orleans. According to audio obtained by Status News, Vega decided to speak candidly about her experience despite initially being "scared" to do so.

"It's not that I just lost a job. There is a lot at stake," Vega said, per Status. "Sometimes you got to be scared and do it still."

CBS NEWS FIRES '60 MINUTES' CORRESPONDENTS, TOP PRODUCER IN SWEEPING SHAKEUP OF STORIED PROGRAM

Vega alleged that while reporting about the anti-ICE unrest in Minnesota in January that spotlighted the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, she was encouraged to also include footage of anti-ICE agitators attacking those that were perceived to be plain-clothed ICE agents, but she concluded there were "no credible examples" despite one reported at the time by Alpha News. She said her team was also asked to include comments made at a press conference by Democratic Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey about him allegedly urging local police to fight ICE agents and that the police chief rolled his eyes in reaction, insisting the moment was "misinformation" after a thorough search.

"That never happened," Vega reportedly said. "We could not find any instance of the mayor saying something like that."

BARI WEISS ADDRESSES SCOTT PELLEY FIRING IN CBS NEWS STAFF CALL, SAYS IT'S THE ‘PATH THAT HE CHOSE’

At a Jan. 14 press conference, Frey said residents had been asking police officers "to fight ICE agents on the street," denouncing the idea of two government entities "literally fighting one another." The police chief standing beside him can be seen raising his eyebrows in a surprised reaction to the apparent request from residents.

Additionally, Vega claimed she was told to introduce a report about President Donald Trump's war with Iran by saying, "Who is winning the war? Iran is totally outgunned by the United States and Israel" despite being just days into the conflict, a quote she considered an "administration talking point."

When asked if the alleged meddling impacted her reports, Vega replied, "If you watch my pieces, you'd see those examples did not make them in."

CBS SHOOTS DOWN 'POLITICAL INTERFERENCE' CLAIMS IN AFTERMATH OF '60 MINUTES' FIRINGS

While she refrained from citing Weiss by name, Vega said the "new administration at CBS News" was behind the various directives and that she "never had an opportunity to sit down with Bari Weiss one on one" before her firing.

"I don't know why I was fired," Vega said, per Status. "It's been about three months now... and I don't know. I was not given a reason. I still have not been given a reason."

A spokesman for CBS News pointed to a statement previously given to Fox News Digital after Vega first spoke out, saying, "We respect Ms. Vega and her contributions, but her claims are not based in reality."

CBS News also cited a comment Weiss previously told the Wall Street Journal, saying "What’s being called ‘editorial interference’ is in reality the job description of an editor in chief."

Vega was among several top "60 Minutes" staffers who were let go in May, including fellow correspondent Sharyn Alfonsi and executive producer Tanya Simon. Veteran "60 Minutes" correspondent Scott Pelley was also fired after a combative exchange he had at a staff meeting with the show's new executive producer Nick Bilton.

item.title: California trans suspect arrested in mother's killing after neighbor recalls heated argument
item.description: Safford Wolfson, 36, was arrested on suspicion of murdering his mother Angela Caprioli at their Laguna Beach home after being named a person of interest.
item.content:encoded:
A California man was arrested this week in connection with his mother's killing, authorities said.

Angela Caprioli, 61, was found dead Monday at a home in Laguna Beach, according to the Laguna Beach Police Department. The New York Post identified Caprioli and the suspect, Safford Wolfson, as mother and son.

Wolfson, 36, was arrested Thursday on suspicion of murder after investigators previously identified him as a person of interest in the case.

RETIRED MATH PROFESSOR CHARGED AFTER WIFE, AN AIRLINE METEOROLOGIST, FOUND SHOT DEAD: COPS

Police said officers responded to a home in the 1300 block of Dunning Drive shortly after 11 a.m. for a death investigation and found Caprioli deceased.

The circumstances surrounding her death remain under investigation.

Neighbor Dustin Pettit said he witnessed Wolfson and Caprioli engaged in what appeared to be a heated argument at the home days before the alleged killing.

FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED AFTER SUSPECTED HUMAN REMAINS FOUND BURIED AT PROPERTY WHERE HIS FATHER LIVED

"I saw her outside talking with him and it seemed like a pretty hostile conversation," Pettit told The California Post.

"She turned around and went inside and slammed the door, like she was fed up with whatever was going on."

"He was pretty mysterious. He wasn't talking to us, you know, he would come outside, smoke a cigarette and play some guitar," he said. "That's kinda the extent of the relationship we've had with him over the last six months or so."

item.title: House Republicans confront NJ governor over 6,600 noncitizens registered to vote in alleged software failure
item.description: House Republicans demand answers from Gov. Miki Sherrill after 6,600 noncitizens were registered to vote through a New Jersey motor vehicle system error.
item.content:encoded:
Nineteen House Republicans are demanding answers from New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill on how approximately 6,600 self-identified noncitizens were registered to vote and cast 400 ballots in what the state described as a software failure.

The group put the question to Sherrill in a letter published on Friday afternoon.

"Despite those answers, a software failure reportedly transmitted their information for voter registration between June 2023 and June 2024. This was not a minor clerical discrepancy," the group wrote in the letter. "It was a catastrophic breakdown of the most basic safeguard in our election system: ensuring that only eligible American citizens are registered and permitted to vote. How do you know this was just a software glitch and not a nefarious act?"

The letter continues to underscore Republican-led concerns that lawmakers are inviting election security liabilities without passing legislation to shore up voter identification and implement federal standards to ensure proof of citizenship.

GOP ERUPTS OVER 6,600 NONCITIZEN VOTERS FOUND IN BLUE STATE AS SCANDAL DEEPENS: ‘WORSE THAN ANYONE EXPECTED’

Its signatories included Rep. Jefferson Van Drew, R-N.J., and Rep. Chris Smith, R-N.J., two of New Jersey’s three Republican congressmen.

Notably, the third, Rep. Tom Kean Jr., R-N.J., did not join.

The system failure originally came to the public’s attention when Sherrill disclosed the issue in an announcement on Tuesday.

"Last week I learned that a serious software error in New Jersey’s Motor Vehicle System led to the registration of roughly 6,600 people who indicated that they were not U.S. citizens between June 2023 and June 2024, almost three years prior to my taking office," Sherrill said.

NEW JERSEY REMOVES 6,600 PEOPLE FROM VOTER ROLLS WHO WERE ELIGIBLE TO CAST A BALLOT FOR 2024 ELECTION

"These individuals answered ‘no’ when asked on a keypad whether they were a U.S. citizen when applying for drivers' licenses and identification cards, but through no fault of their own, the system registered them anyway."

Republicans in their letter listed a series of questions they said the state should answer, including what testing it normally conducts for voter roll maintenance, the specific counties where the improper ballots were cast, and whether Sherrill’s administration would support voter-ID legislation.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"Republicans have been sounding the alarm for years about weaknesses in voter-registration systems, inadequate voter-roll maintenance, and the danger that noncitizens may be registered and permitted to vote in national elections, which is illegal under federal law," the letter stated.

The group has requested a response to its questions no later than Aug. 21, 2026.
